question: What is a JWT and what is it made of?
title: JWT Structure Explained – Java Backend Security Interview
direct_answer: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact, URL-safe token used for securely transmitting information between parties. It consists of three Base64URL-encoded parts separated by dots: Header.Payload.Signature. The header specifies the algorithm (like HS256), the payload contains claims (user data, expiry), and the signature verifies integrity using a secret key.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JWT structure and its role in stateless authentication
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the payload is encrypted — it's only base64-encoded and readable by anyone who decodes it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Proactively clarify that JWT provides integrity through the signature, not confidentiality — never put passwords or sensitive secrets in the payload

sections.title: Understanding JWT Structure and Purpose
sections.content: A **JSON Web Token (JWT)** is like a tamper-proof digital passport. Imagine you check into a hotel and receive a wristband with your name, room number, and checkout date printed on it. Anyone can read the wristband, but the hotel's special hologram sticker proves it's authentic. JWT works the same way: it's a compact token carrying user information that anyone can decode and read, but only the server with the secret key can create or verify the authenticity signature. This makes JWT perfect for **stateless authentication** in REST APIs — the server doesn't need to store sessions because all the information travels with each request. The token has three parts joined by dots: the **Header** (algorithm metadata), **Payload** (user claims like userId and expiry), and **Signature** (cryptographic proof of integrity). All three parts are Base64URL-encoded for safe transmission in URLs and HTTP headers.

sections.title: Creating and Validating a JWT in Spring Boot
Key Points
content: **Three-part structure**: Header (algorithm), Payload (claims), Signature (integrity proof) — all Base64URL-encoded and joined by dots
**Base64 is not encryption**: Anyone can decode the payload and read the claims — never store passwords or credit card numbers in JWT
**Signature verification**: Only the server with the secret key can generate valid signatures — tampering with payload breaks the signature
**Stateless authentication**: Server doesn't store sessions — all user context travels in the token itself, making horizontal scaling easier
**Claims**: Payload contains standard claims like sub (subject/username), iat (issued at), exp (expiration), and custom claims you define
**Compact format**: URL-safe and small enough to fit in HTTP headers, unlike XML-based SAML tokens
**Self-contained**: The token carries all information needed for authorization decisions — no database lookup required on every request

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A JWT is a token format for securely passing information between a client and server. It's made of three parts separated by dots: the header, the payload, and the signature. The header tells you what algorithm was used, like HS256. The payload contains claims, which are just key-value pairs of user data — things like the username, user ID, and when the token expires. The signature is created by hashing the header and payload together with a secret key that only the server knows. Here's the important part that trips people up: the payload is base64-encoded, not encrypted. That means anyone can decode it and read what's inside. The signature doesn't hide the data — it just proves the token hasn't been tampered with. If someone changes even one character in the payload, the signature won't match anymore and the server will reject it. So you'd never put a password or credit card number in a JWT because it's readable by anyone. The whole point is to make authentication stateless. The server doesn't need to store session data because the token itself carries everything needed to identify and authorize the user. That makes it perfect for REST APIs where you want to scale horizontally without sticky sessions.

beats.label: three parts
beats.content: A JWT is three Base64URL-encoded sections separated by dots. The header declares the signing algorithm (HS256 or RS256). The payload carries claims: the user's ID, email, roles, when the token was issued (iat), and when it expires (exp). The signature is an HMAC or RSA hash of the header and payload using a secret key.

beats.label: the big misconception
beats.content: The payload is not encrypted. It's just Base64 encoded. Anyone who intercepts a JWT can decode the payload and read every claim in it. The signature only proves the token hasn't been tampered with — it says nothing about confidentiality. So never put passwords, credit card numbers, or sensitive PII in a JWT payload.

beats.label: candidates miss
beats.content: candidates miss: saying the JWT is 'encrypted' or 'secure' without qualification. The correct statement is: the signature verifies integrity, not confidentiality. The payload is readable by anyone.

question: How does JWT-based authentication work in a Spring Boot REST API?
title: JWT Authentication Flow in Spring Boot REST API
direct_answer: JWT authentication in Spring Boot works through a login endpoint that validates credentials and returns a signed JWT. A custom filter (extending OncePerRequestFilter) intercepts every request, extracts the JWT from the Authorization header, validates the signature, and sets the authenticated user in SecurityContextHolder. The session management is configured as STATELESS so no session data is stored on the server.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical implementation knowledge of JWT in Spring Security, not just theoretical understanding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing JWT in isolation without mentioning the filter chain, SecurityContext, or STATELESS session policy
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the key components by role: JwtUtil for token operations, JwtAuthenticationFilter extending OncePerRequestFilter, SecurityConfig setting sessionCreationPolicy to STATELESS

sections.title: JWT Authentication Flow in Spring Boot
sections.content: Think of JWT authentication like a movie theater where you buy a ticket once (login), then show that ticket to enter the theater and buy concessions without re-proving your identity. In Spring Boot, the flow has two phases. **Phase 1 (Login)**: User sends credentials to /auth/login endpoint. The controller validates username and password, and if correct, generates a JWT containing the user's identity and expiry time. This token is returned to the client. **Phase 2 (Authenticated Requests)**: For every subsequent API call, the client includes the JWT in the Authorization header as "Bearer <token>". A custom **JwtAuthenticationFilter** intercepts the request before it reaches your controller, extracts the token, validates the signature using the secret key, and if valid, loads the user details and sets them in **SecurityContextHolder**. From that point forward, Spring Security treats the request as authenticated. The key architectural difference from session-based auth: the server stores nothing. The JWT itself carries all the state, making the API **stateless** and horizontally scalable.

sections.title: JWT Authentication Filter Implementation
Key Points
content: **Login endpoint**: POST /auth/login validates credentials, calls JwtUtil.generateToken, returns JWT to client — this is the only place tokens are created
**JwtAuthenticationFilter**: Extends OncePerRequestFilter to intercept every request exactly once, extracts token from Authorization header, validates signature
**SecurityContextHolder**: Acts as thread-local storage for the authenticated user — once set by the filter, @PreAuthorize and @Secured annotations work downstream
**STATELESS session policy**: SecurityConfig sets sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS) so Spring Security never creates HttpSession — pure token-based auth
**Filter ordering**: JwtAuthenticationFilter must run before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter in the filter chain — configured in SecurityFilterChain
**No database lookup per request**: Optional optimization — if claims contain roles, you can skip UserDetailsService call and build authorities directly from JWT
**Authorization header format**: Client sends "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..." — the word Bearer is a convention indicating token-based auth

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JWT authentication in Spring Boot happens in two steps. First, there's a login endpoint, usually something like POST /auth/login. The user sends their username and password. If the credentials are valid, the server generates a JWT using a utility class — let's call it JwtUtil — that signs the token with a secret key and includes the username and expiration time. The server returns this token to the client. From that point on, for every API request, the client includes the JWT in the Authorization header with the format Bearer followed by the token. Now here's the Spring Security part. You create a custom filter that extends OncePerRequestFilter. This filter runs on every incoming request before it reaches your controllers. It pulls the JWT from the Authorization header, validates the signature by calling JwtUtil, and if the token is valid, extracts the username. Then it loads the user's details and authorities, and sets them in SecurityContextHolder. That's Spring Security's way of saying this request is authenticated. One pitfall: you have to configure Spring Security with a STATELESS session policy. Otherwise it'll try to create HTTP sessions, which defeats the whole purpose of using JWT. The result is a fully stateless API where the server doesn't store anything about logged-in users — all the state travels in the token.

Spring Security then sees an authenticated principal and lets the request reach the controller.

beats.content: sharp edge: forgetting to set SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS and forgetting to disable CSRF. Without STATELESS, Spring creates a session anyway. Without disabling CSRF, form submissions break. These two lines must go in your SecurityConfig.

question: What are the security risks of using JWT and how do you mitigate them?
title: JWT Security Risks and Mitigations – Java Backend
direct_answer: JWT security risks include algorithm confusion attacks (accepting alg:none), secret key leakage, lack of built-in token revocation, exposing sensitive data in the readable payload, XSS attacks when stored in localStorage, and tokens with no expiry. Mitigations: enforce strong algorithms, rotate secrets regularly, use short expiry with refresh tokens, store only non-sensitive claims, prefer HttpOnly cookies, and implement a token blacklist for critical revocations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Security maturity beyond basic JWT usage — understanding where JWT can fail and how to defend against attacks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming JWT is secure by default without considering algorithm attacks, storage vulnerabilities, or revocation challenges
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the alg:none vulnerability explicitly — it's a JWT-specific attack where the server accepts unsigned tokens if you don't validate the algorithm

sections.title: JWT Security Risks and Defense Strategies
sections.content: JWT is not secure by magic — it's a format that requires careful implementation to avoid critical vulnerabilities. Think of JWT like a driver's license: anyone can see the information on it, and if you leave it lying around or if the issuing authority's security is weak, it can be forged or misused. The biggest risks come from **algorithm confusion** (tricking the server into accepting unsigned tokens), **secret key compromise** (if leaked, attackers can forge valid tokens), **no revocation mechanism** (you can't invalidate a token before expiry without extra infrastructure), **sensitive data exposure** (the payload is base64-encoded, not encrypted), and **client-side storage vulnerabilities** (XSS attacks if stored in localStorage). Additionally, tokens with long or infinite expiry become permanent keys if stolen. Each risk has a corresponding mitigation: validate algorithms explicitly, protect and rotate secret keys, use short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens, store only non-sensitive identifiers in the payload, and use HttpOnly cookies with SameSite attributes for storage.

sections.title: Secure JWT Validation with Algorithm Enforcement
Key Points
content: **Algorithm confusion attack**: Attacker changes header to alg:none or alg:HS256 to bypass signature — always validate the algorithm explicitly using requireAlgorithm
**Secret key security**: Store secret in environment variables or vault, never commit to Git — rotate periodically and use strong keys (256+ bits for HS256)
**No built-in revocation**: JWT can't be invalidated before expiry — use short TTL (15-60 min) and maintain a blacklist cache (Redis) for critical revocations like logout
**Payload visibility**: Base64 encoding is NOT encryption — never store passwords, credit cards, or PII — store only user ID and roles
**Client storage vulnerability**: localStorage is vulnerable to XSS — prefer HttpOnly cookies with SameSite=Strict to prevent both XSS and CSRF
**Expiry hygiene**: Never create tokens without exp claim — set reasonable expiry (access tokens short, refresh tokens longer but rotatable)
**Signature algorithm strength**: Use HS256 (HMAC-SHA256) minimum for symmetric or RS256 (RSA-SHA256) for asymmetric — never accept none or HS1

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JWT has several security risks you need to know about. The first is algorithm confusion. An attacker can change the header to say alg:none and if your validation code doesn't explicitly check the algorithm, the server might accept an unsigned token. That's a critical vulnerability. You prevent this by using requireAlgorithm in your parser and never trusting the header's algorithm claim alone. Second risk is secret key compromise. If your secret key leaks, anyone can forge valid tokens. You mitigate this by storing the secret in environment variables or a vault, never hardcoding it, and rotating it periodically. Third, JWT has no built-in revocation. Once you issue a token, it's valid until expiry. If a user logs out or you need to ban an account, the token still works. The solution is to use short expiry times — like fifteen minutes for access tokens — and keep a blacklist in Redis for cases where you absolutely need to revoke early. Fourth, the payload isn't encrypted. Anyone can base64-decode it and read what's inside. So you never put sensitive data like passwords or credit card numbers in there — just user ID and roles. Fifth, if you store JWT in localStorage on the client, it's vulnerable to XSS attacks. A better approach is HttpOnly cookies with SameSite set to Strict. That prevents JavaScript from accessing the token and mitigates CSRF. The key point is that JWT is just a format. It doesn't make your app secure automatically. You have to implement these defenses deliberately.

beats.label: the risks
beats.content:
The main vulnerabilities:
- Algorithm confusion (alg:none): attacker sets the header algorithm to 'none' and the server skips signature verification — explicitly whitelist your expected algorithm
- Secret compromise: if the HS256 secret leaks, every token can be forged — use RS256 for high-value systems
- No revocation: a stolen token is valid until it expires — use short expiry (15-60 min) and refresh tokens
- Sensitive data in payload: the payload is Base64 encoded, not encrypted — visible to anyone
- localStorage storage: XSS can steal the token — use HttpOnly cookie instead

beats.label: the mitigations
beats.content: Use the jjwt library which enforces algorithm whitelisting. Set expiry (exp claim) on every token. Store tokens in HttpOnly cookies with SameSite=Strict. Pair short access tokens with longer-lived refresh tokens in your database for revocation capability.

beats.label: non-obvious
beats.content: non-obvious: the alg:none attack is specific to JWT and not widely known outside security circles. Mentioning it by name in an interview signals genuine security awareness, not just tutorial knowledge.

question: Where should you store a JWT on the client side?
title: Where to Store JWT on Client Side – Security Tradeoffs
direct_answer: The best place to store JWT on the client is in an HttpOnly cookie with SameSite=Strict attribute. This prevents XSS attacks (JavaScript can't access the cookie) and mitigates CSRF (SameSite blocks cross-site requests). LocalStorage and sessionStorage are vulnerable to XSS. Memory storage (JavaScript variable) is secure but lost on page refresh. Avoid localStorage despite its convenience.

interviewer_intent.testing: Security awareness of client-side storage options and their attack surface tradeoffs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Recommending localStorage because it's simple — interviewers watch for this as a red flag indicating lack of security awareness
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Articulate the full tradeoff: HttpOnly cookies sacrifice XSS exposure for CSRF risk, which we mitigate with SameSite or CSRF tokens — showing you understand the security reasoning

sections.title: Client-Side JWT Storage Options and Security Tradeoffs
sections.content: Where you store a JWT on the client determines what attacks you're vulnerable to. Think of it like choosing where to hide a spare house key: under the doormat (easy but obvious), in a lockbox (harder but still accessible), or not having a spare at all (most secure but inconvenient). **LocalStorage** and **sessionStorage** are the "under the doormat" options — convenient because any JavaScript can access them, but that's exactly why they're dangerous. If an attacker injects malicious script through XSS, they can steal the token instantly. **HttpOnly cookies** are like the lockbox: JavaScript can't access them, so XSS attacks can't steal the token. But cookies are automatically sent with every request to the domain, reintroducing **CSRF vulnerability** — an attacker can trick your browser into making authenticated requests. You mitigate CSRF with **SameSite=Strict** or by adding CSRF tokens. **Memory storage** (keeping the token in a JavaScript variable) is the most secure because it's inaccessible to both XSS and CSRF, but the token is lost on page refresh, requiring re-login.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Storage Strategy
sections.content: **Use HttpOnly cookies with SameSite=Strict** for most production applications. This provides the best balance: JavaScript can't access the token (blocking XSS theft), and SameSite prevents cross-site request forgery. Configure the cookie with Secure flag in production to enforce HTTPS. Set the path to /api so the token is only sent to backend endpoints, not static assets. This is the approach used by major platforms like GitHub and Google. **Use memory storage** for high-security applications where you can't afford any token theft risk — think banking apps. The trade-off is that users must re-authenticate on every page refresh, so you'll need to explain this UX to stakeholders. Pair it with a long-lived refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie to balance security and experience. **Avoid localStorage** entirely for JWT — the XSS risk is too high. Even with CSP (Content Security Policy) headers, one missed sanitization can leak all tokens. localStorage is acceptable only for non-sensitive data like UI preferences.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **localStorage vulnerability**: Any XSS attack can execute document.cookie or localStorage.getItem to steal tokens — one unsanitized input field can compromise all logged-in users
**HttpOnly cookie protection**: The HttpOnly flag makes cookies inaccessible to JavaScript — even if attacker injects script, they can't read the cookie value
**SameSite attribute**: SameSite=Strict blocks cookies on cross-site requests — prevents CSRF where attacker tricks your browser into authenticated requests
**CSRF mitigation strategy**: Combine HttpOnly cookies with either SameSite=Strict (blocks cross-site) or CSRF tokens (validate origin)
**Memory storage tradeoff**: Most secure but least convenient — token lost on refresh, requires refresh token flow or re-login
**Cookie configuration**: Set Secure (HTTPS only), HttpOnly (no JS), SameSite=Strict (no cross-site), and appropriate Path (/api) and Domain
**CSP headers**: Content Security Policy can reduce XSS surface but doesn't eliminate it — still prefer HttpOnly over localStorage

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You should store JWT in an HttpOnly cookie with the SameSite attribute set to Strict. Here's why. localStorage is the most common answer, but it's actually the worst option from a security perspective. If an attacker manages to inject malicious JavaScript through an XSS vulnerability — maybe through an unsanitized comment field or search input — that script can immediately access localStorage and steal all the tokens. Then the attacker can impersonate users. With an HttpOnly cookie, JavaScript can't access it at all. Even if the attacker injects a script, they can't read the cookie value. That blocks the XSS attack path. Now HttpOnly cookies introduce a different problem: CSRF, or cross-site request forgery. Cookies are automatically sent with every request to your domain, so an attacker could trick your browser into making authenticated requests from their malicious site. That's where SameSite comes in. SameSite equals Strict tells the browser never to send this cookie on cross-site requests. So even if you click a malicious link, the cookie won't be attached and the request won't be authenticated. Some teams also use memory storage, which means keeping the token in a JavaScript variable. That's secure because it's not accessible to other sites and disappears on XSS attacks from other origins, but the token is lost every time you refresh the page. You'd have to re-login constantly unless you pair it with a refresh token. Bottom line: HttpOnly cookies with SameSite equals Strict give you the best security with acceptable user experience.

beats.content: production trap: recommending localStorage because it's the default in every tutorial. Interviewers know this is the insecure path. State the XSS risk explicitly and recommend HttpOnly cookie instead.

question: How do you handle JWT expiry and token refresh?
title: JWT Expiry and Token Refresh – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: JWT expiry is handled with two token types: short-lived access tokens (15-60 minutes) for API requests, and long-lived refresh tokens (days to weeks) stored securely. When the access token expires, the client sends the refresh token to a /auth/refresh endpoint, receives a new access token, and retries the failed request. Refresh token rotation (invalidating the old refresh token on each use) prevents replay attacks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of production-grade token lifecycle management beyond basic JWT issuance
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting long expiry on access tokens to avoid refresh complexity — defeats the security purpose of short-lived tokens
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe the complete flow including refresh token rotation, where each refresh invalidates the previous refresh token to prevent reuse if stolen

sections.title: Token Expiry and Refresh Mechanism
sections.content: Token expiry is the balance between security and user experience. Imagine your office access card expires every hour for security reasons, but re-registering every hour would be miserable. The solution: you carry both a short-term **access card** (expires in 1 hour) and a long-term **ID badge** (valid for weeks) that you only show to security to get a fresh access card when needed. JWT works the same way. **Access tokens** are short-lived (15-60 minutes) and used on every API request. If stolen, the attacker has limited time to cause damage. **Refresh tokens** are long-lived (days or weeks), stored more securely (HttpOnly cookie), and used only to obtain new access tokens from a dedicated /auth/refresh endpoint. When an API request returns 401 Unauthorized due to expired access token, the client automatically calls /auth/refresh with the refresh token, receives a new access token, and retries the original request — all transparent to the user. To prevent refresh token theft, implement **refresh token rotation**: each time a refresh token is used, invalidate it and issue a new one.

sections.title: Token Refresh Flow Implementation
Key Points
content: **Two-token strategy**: Access tokens (short TTL, 15-60 min) for API requests + refresh tokens (long TTL, 7-30 days) for getting new access tokens
**Silent refresh**: When API returns 401, the client automatically calls /auth/refresh with the refresh token, gets new access token, retries original request — user never sees the error
**Refresh token rotation**: Each use of a refresh token invalidates it and issues a new one — prevents replay attacks if old refresh token is stolen
**Storage separation**: Access token can live in memory (JS variable), refresh token in HttpOnly cookie — limits exposure surface
**Refresh token persistence**: Refresh tokens must be stored server-side (database) with user ID, expiry, and revocation status — enables logout across devices
**Expiry balance**: Too short (5 min access) annoys users with frequent refreshes — too long (24 hours) gives attackers too much time — 15-60 min is typical
**Revocation on logout**: Logout endpoint must delete the refresh token from database — otherwise the user appears logged out but their tokens still work

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: JWT expiry is handled using two types of tokens: access tokens and refresh tokens. The access token is what you send with every API request, and it has a short lifespan — typically fifteen to sixty minutes. The refresh token is much longer-lived — maybe a week or two — and it's used only to get new access tokens. Here's how the flow works. When the user logs in, you give them both tokens. The access token goes in memory or a JavaScript variable, and the refresh token goes in an HttpOnly cookie for extra security. Now let's say the user is browsing your app and an API call fails with a 401 because the access token expired. The client code catches that, makes a request to a dedicated refresh endpoint — something like POST /auth/refresh — and sends the refresh token. If the refresh token is still valid, the server generates a new access token and sends it back. The client stores this new access token and retries the original API call. All of this happens automatically behind the scenes, so the user doesn't even notice. One important security measure is refresh token rotation. Every time you use a refresh token to get a new access token, you invalidate the old refresh token and issue a new one. That way, if an attacker steals a refresh token, it's only useful once. A common mistake is making the access token super long-lived to avoid implementing this refresh flow. But that defeats the purpose. If someone steals an access token with a twenty-four-hour expiry, they have a full day to do damage. Short expiry limits that window.

seo.metaDescription: JWT expiry handling with refresh tokens. Short-lived access tokens, long-lived refresh tokens in HttpOnly cookie. Refresh token rotation for theft detection.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with OWASP-compliant security
speakable_v2.hook: Short-lived tokens expire and users shouldn't have to re-login. The refresh token pattern solves this cleanly.

beats.label: two token model
beats.content: At login, issue two tokens. The access token is short-lived (15-30 minutes) and used in the Authorization header for every API call. The refresh token is long-lived (7-30 days), stored in an HttpOnly cookie, and used only to obtain a new access token.

beats.label: refresh flow
beats.content: When the access token expires, the API returns 401. The client silently POSTs to /auth/refresh with the refresh token cookie. The server validates it exists in the database and hasn't expired, then issues a new access token and rotates the refresh token (old one is invalidated). If a rotated token is reused, it signals theft — invalidate all refresh tokens for that user.

beats.label: gotcha
beats.content: gotcha: setting access tokens to 7-day expiry 'to keep things simple.' That defeats the security benefit of short-lived tokens. The refresh complexity exists for a reason — stolen access tokens should expire quickly.
